persistedClaim.text: Wai Wah Tsang uses a gym-membership analogy: accepting a university offer is like joining a gym -- the outcome still depends on how the student uses what is available.

record.text: Um, thank you so much for the question. And, um, I'll, I'll break that question down, uh, so it's, uh, so it's more, you know, kind of digestible. And I think the first thing, you know, about, uh, that, uh, that age-old question that I, I receive from, you know, parents and from students, uh, about, you know, "Will I get a job?" or "Will my child get a job?" And I think whilst it's a really completely understandable question about the return of investments, I think that we have to be honest. And the most honest answer is, no university can guarantee, uh, that a student is guaranteed employment. Um, but I think what we can say, uh, especially from a Warwick perspective, is that universities can provide opportunities, they can support, um, support networks, and the relevant experiences, um, to significantly improve a student's, you know, chances and prospects and, and, and engagement. And when we look at things like around, you know, career and employability, I think, um, we need to move, you know, beyond, you know, the idea that the degree alone is actually going to be, uh, the, the guarantee to, to get a job. And when we're looking at the job market, you know, employers are actually not just looking for degrees that are linear, you know. They are looking for a bit more, uh, interdisciplinary. They are looking for, you know, uh, outside thinkers of the, of the normal discipline. And I think that having that combination, uh, of course, you know, students are going to need to continue to do well, uh, in terms of their academic achievements, um, but we're, we're seeing lots more degrees, you know, having, uh, practical elements, lot more placements, and a lot more internship opportunities, where students can continue to, uh, you know, develop their skills, um, and, you know, it's, it's the platform that we're trying to give and that support, so it allows students to, um, enhance, uh, their kind of ability and to articulate their strengths. Um, and I think that when we're looking at students, um, those who utilize, you know, those opportunities, you know, those who are actively, uh, engage with internships, placements, um, extracurricular activities whilst they're at university, but also, you know, utilize, um, rely on the strengths that they've, uh, they've had from school and bringing it forward, you know, demonstrating their leadership opportunities, and utilizing that support, they're the ones who are actually seen to be, um, you know, the most successful moving forward. And I think that, you know, universities like, uh, you know, like mine, like the University of Warwick, you know, one of our strengths is that, you know, the combination of having that academic excellence and having a strong employer reputation, uh, but also having, uh, extensive, uh, industry engagements. And I think that, you know, our engagement over the last 40 years, that we've had with employers, uh, and, and building those relationships across many sectors, um, I think that students can benefit, uh, or increase their chances of, of trying to get a successful, you know, career. And, you know, we, we try to do that through building good stories, building successful stories where we can, uh, and that could be across, you know, our, um, extensive global, uh, alumni network, where we've currently just surpassed 320,000, uh, students, and there are over 85,000, um, 8,500, uh, Indian alumni, who's, who's walked through those doors. So, I think it's really important that we continue to build the profile of the students and increase their chances of employability, but also whilst they're studying. Um, so, you asked, I think, you asked the question around kind of, you know, the right fit, what university is the right fit. And I think that, you know, we always encourage counselors, uh, to engage with the students and, and families, and, and to think about, yes, it's about the right fit, not always about which university is the highest-ranked. Um, and I think that giving the student, you know, the right opportunities, uh, to not just survive but also to thrive, um, that's where I think students are going to get the most of their academic education. You know, they, they need to be academically challenged, they need to be, uh, need to have that support system, whether it's through education or through the careers, whether it's through their personal tutor or through their professors, for example. But also they need to stay motivated as well. And also to make the most of the opportunities that are given to them. And I think that, you know, students need to ask themselves, "Yes, this university might be the highest-ranked, but it's not a campus university, or it's a city-based university." And those things, you know, they need to ask themselves, "Which environment am I going to, you know, is going to suit me the best?" Um, and there's also, also other things as well, you know, looking at the, uh, interdisciplinary learning, you know, looking at the broad range of, uh, societies that are available. And I think it's really, really important to focus on that because what do societies have anything to do with employability? Well, employers are looking for, you know, your soft skills, and your communication skills, your networking skills and things like that. And these are easy wins. These are easy ways to learn a skill, learn an experience by doing something, but not being very, um, shall I say, you're not focused on it, because you're making, you know, friends. Those are transferable skills. And if you're getting jobs within societies, you know, you might be a treasurer, you might be the vice president or president, that's something that, uh, those skills and that networking, that they can transfer into, you know, the kind of the working world. So, it's, it's about building your profile as you go along. Um, and so, there's one thing that I, I normally say, um, to, to anyone is that, if students get an offer, and they have been accepted, I always use this gym analogy, that, if you go, if you've been accepted and enrolled at a university, you have to ask yourself, "Okay, look at the, I need to get these opportunities now." So, if you go to the gym, you can basically go there and just be a member, and you can just do the bare minimum, and you can come out three or four years, and you can say, "Okay, I was a member of that gym." But in order to stress yourself, in order to progress, you need to utilize the equipment that that, that's available there. And if you don't put in the work, you're not going to get the returns, and you're not going to achieve the goals that you're particularly looking for. Uh, so, that's my analogy. Hopefully, it's relatable to some people. Um, I think that when, when students are looking again at the, the rankings, I think it's really important for counselors and students to look at the rankings, but not just for the current year, and not even the last two or three years. In my opinion, I think that it's important to look at consistency. And we're looking at consistency, well, what comes with consistency? It comes with long-standing values, it comes, um, academic, uh, excellence, whether it's teaching excellence or research excellence or both, or a strong reputation. And I think that if you can combine all of that, then, what employers, uh, uh, looking for in their candidates, and all the opportunities that you get, hopefully, that's something that, uh, will make them stand out when that process comes. So, yeah, I think the, you know, the, the reality of today's, um, graduate market is that, you know, employers are looking for talented students, looking for well-rounded students from a whole host or a range of, uh, institutions. And I think, um, what makes them stand out, what makes them different is how they use their university experience. So, to, to, to summarize, it's not about, um, you know, "will my child" or "will I get a job" at the end of it, but I think it's, you know, "what does the university offer for me" or "offer my child?" What type of environment, what type of opportunities, and what support is there, you know, to develop, um, the, the, the graduate in a competitive market? And I think that finding the right university is, is really critical in this space. Um, so, hopefully, that answers the, the question in, in some way.
